Coronary Heart Disease Prediction

Project Inroduction

My lab results showed abnormal cholesterol and triglyceride levels, and my doctor informed me that I am at increased risk. For this reason, I chose this topic. The initial project plan included performing population parameter analysis as well, but conducting the regression alone took a significant amount of time, so those analyses were ultimately excluded.

The main challenge of the project came from the NHANES sample design. Because of the complex multistage sampling approach, NHANES assigns different weights to different variables and subsamples. Understanding this design and selecting the correct weights was the most difficult and time-consuming part of the project.

In summary, this project aims to predict coronary heart disease using high-density cholesterol, low-density cholesterol, and triglycerides.

Data Introduction.

In 2021–2023, individuals participated in NHANES interviews and medical examinations. The NHANES program uses a multistage sampling design that intentionally oversamples people with certain characteristics, such as specific racial/ethnic groups or age categories. Because of this design—and for other methodological reasons—NHANES assigns different sampling weights to different variables and subsamples. For more information about the sample design and weighting procedures, please refer to the source provided below.

Five datasets were downloaded from the NHANES website and merged using the participant sequence number (SEQN):

DEMO_L.csv – demographic information
HDL_L.csv – high-density cholesterol measurements
TRIGLY_L.csv – low-density cholesterol and triglyceride measurements
TCHOL_L.csv – total cholesterol measurements
MCQ_L.csv – self-reported history of angina, heart attack, or cardiovascular disease

The suffix “_L” indicates that the data come from the 2021–2023 cycle. These files have different numbers of rows because only a subset of interview respondents participate in particular laboratory tests. DEMO_L.csv contains the largest number of rows since all participants provide demographic information.

For details on data preprocessing, please refer to the two preprocessing scripts included in the project folder.

Logistic Regression

In this section, we try to predict if a person has a coronary heart disease.

Logistic Regression Without Using Weights

In the beginning, I ignored the various weights in the dataset because I couldn’t figure out what they meant and how to use them. However, my models produced AUC around 5. I thought the poor result was because of the missing weights so I decided to use weights to improve the result. However, when I were writing this file, I found out that the low AUC was because of a bug in my original code. After correcting the bug, the ROC looks normal. The corrected result is provided below.

Training with 3 predictors

# -----model with multiple predictors-----------.
# 1. Fit on training set
model <- glm(
  coronary ~ high_density_level + low_density_level + triglyceride_level,
  family = binomial,
  data = train
)

# 2. Predict on *validation* set
validation$prob <- predict(
  model,
  newdata = validation,
  type = "response"
)

# 3. ROC on validation set

g <- roc(response = validation$coronary,
         predictor = validation$prob)
## Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
## Setting direction: controls < cases
g
## 
## Call:
## roc.default(response = validation$coronary, predictor = validation$prob)
## 
## Data: validation$prob in 961 controls (validation$coronary 0) < 60 cases (validation$coronary 1).
## Area under the curve: 0.7247
plot(g)

Logistic Regression With Weights

Because of low AUC values due to the bug and my belief that it was caused by ignoring weights, I decided to integrate weights in the regression. In order to learn how to use them, I studied NAHNAES’s sample design, a concept that I haven’t studied before and struggled to understand. Another challenge was to choose a weight since there were two weights in the dataset. It took me a while to understand the criteria - choose the weight for the smallest subsample if multiple subsamples are used in the analysis. In my case, I needed to decide which subsample was smaller because I had two: the phlebotomy subsample(people who gave blood specimen) and the fasting subsample (people who were asked to fast). It took me several hours just to decide on this. Finally, I found out that fasting subsample was smaller because people in the sample fasted first and then gave blood specimen.

Logistic Regression With Using Weight_2(Fasting Subsample Weight)

In the beginning,the models couldn’t converge, no matter the number of predictors that I used. This turned out to be another bug that I didn’t notice I thought the failure was due to lack of datapoints in the subsample because the fasting subsample was the smallest subsample. However, somehow, the models could converge after some changes that I made, but I lost track of what change I made.

Regression with weight 2 was presented below. In order to use weight, svydesign() must be used to construct the design object and this object need to be used in the regression.

Fitting a model 3 predictors

# --------- model with 3 predictors -----------------------
# train model on the train set
model1 <- svyglm(
  coronary ~ high_density_level +low_density_level +triglyceride_level  ,
  design = design_train_sub,
  family = quasibinomial()
)

# predict on the validation set.

val_df <- design_validation_sub$variables
val_df$predicted <- predict(model1, newdata = val_df, type = "response")

roc_val_three <- roc(
  response = val_df$coronary,
  predictor = val_df$predicted,
  weights = val_df$weight_2
)
## Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
## Setting direction: controls < cases
roc_val_three
## 
## Call:
## roc.default(response = val_df$coronary, predictor = val_df$predicted,     weights = val_df$weight_2)
## 
## Data: val_df$predicted in 970 controls (val_df$coronary 0) < 59 cases (val_df$coronary 1).
## Area under the curve: 0.7521
plot(roc_val_three)

Logistic Regression With Using Weight_1(Phlebotomy Subsample Weight)

Since my initial attempts to use weight_2(fast subsample weight), the Phlebotomy weight was used because it was the weight for the second smallest subsample and also our only choice left.

Conclusion

Even though NHANHE used multistage sampling to oversample certain subgroups the population and they emphasize that weights should be used regression, the impact of not using the weights or using a less ideal weight doesn’t have much impact on the prediction results. For a logistic regression with one variable low_density_level, there is not much differences in the AUC value of the fitted models, whether the model used weights or used different weight not.

For the last model,a SLR with weight_1, we choose a threshhold that yields the highest accuracy.

# 1.choose the best threshold for this model and calculate the accuracy. 

roc_obj <- roc(response = val_df$coronary, predictor = val_df$predicted)
## Setting levels: control = 0, case = 1
## Setting direction: controls < cases
best <- coords(roc_obj, "best", best.method="closest.topleft")
best
##    threshold specificity sensitivity
## 1 0.06707157   0.7651435   0.6271186
best_threshold <- as.numeric(best$threshold)

# 2. predicted classes using optimal threshold
val_df$predicted_labels <- ifelse(val_df$predicted >= best_threshold[], 1, 0)

# 3. accuracy
accuracy <- mean(val_df$predicted_labels == val_df$coronary)
accuracy
## [1] 0.757
